answer.label: Not Augustine of Hippo — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: Modern wording seen online by 2013 · Spurgeon’s lion image: 1875 and 1888
answer.sourceLine: No one has found this line in any of Augustine’s works, and Wikiquote lists it as misattributed ↗. Its closest documented ancestor is the Baptist preacher Charles Spurgeon, who said the Bible was like a caged lion that needed no defenders: “Open that door! Let the lord of the forest come forth free” (sermon, 22 January 1888 ↗). The snappy “truth” version is anonymous and modern.

source.heading: The closest real source: Spurgeon’s caged lion

docMeta.dd: The Lover of God’s Law Filled with Peace
No source located in Augustine or Spurgeon

source.excerpt: The Word of God can take care of itself, and will do so if we preach it, and cease defending it. See you that lion. They have caged him for his preservation; shut him up behind iron bars to secure him from his foes! … O fools, and slow of heart! Open that door! Let the lord of the forest come forth free. Who will dare to encounter him? What does he want with your guardian care? Let the pure gospel go forth in all its lion-like majesty, and it will soon clear its own way and ease itself of its adversaries.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Augustine’s Misattributed section ↗ with the note “Not found in Augustine’s works”. It points to Spurgeon’s 1875 Bible Society speech and his 1888 sermon.

The Fauxtations blog (18 October 2015) ↗ searched Augustine’s works at CCEL and in Latin and found nothing close. Google Books showed no reference to the quote before 2014, and the blogger had first seen it on Facebook in 2013.
Trent Horn at Catholic Answers (3 August 2020) ↗: “There is no way St. Augustine said this.” He found no book attributing it to Augustine written before the twenty-first century.
The lion passage is in Spurgeon’s sermon No. 2004, preached 22 January 1888 ↗, published in the Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit, vol. 34.
source.excerptNote: Spurgeon is talking about the Bible and the gospel, not truth in general. The compressed “truth is like a lion” wording appears in none of his texts quoted here.

sourceLink.text: Full sermon text at The Spurgeon Library

source.rightsNote: The popular “truth is like a lion” wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author or first publication, so no rights status is asserted. Spurgeon’s 1888 sermon, quoted above, predates 1931 and is not the source of the exact wording.

author.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
author.heading: About Charles Haddon Spurgeon
author.bio: Charles Haddon Spurgeon was an English Particular Baptist preacher known to admirers as the “Prince of Preachers,” and he preached at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, Newington. He repeatedly compared the Bible to a lion that needs releasing, not defending. That image is the closest documented source of the modern saying. He spoke of the Bible and the gospel, though, not of “truth” in general, and the popular wording is not his.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This saying is a favorite on Christian social media and church signs, almost always signed “St. Augustine”. Researchers who searched his works found no trace of it.

items.why: Not in his works. A search of his Latin writings found “lion” (leo) and “truth” (veritas) in the same document 125 times, but never near each other (Fauxtations ↗). Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗.

items.tag: Source of the image, not the words
items.why: Spurgeon did use the lion metaphor, for the Bible and the gospel: “Open that door! Let the lord of the forest come forth free” (1888 sermon ↗). Trent Horn calls the passage “strikingly similar” but notes “it may not be the origin of this quote” (Catholic Answers ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The truth: the line is an anonymous modern compression, seen on Facebook by 2013. Its closest documented ancestor is Spurgeon’s 19th-century lion image for the Bible, and no researcher has found it in Augustine (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why the fake matters
lead: The saying is often used to argue that faith needs no reasoned defense. Catholic apologist Trent Horn calls it his least favorite apocryphal saint quote. He points out that it runs against the biblical call to “make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. 3:15) (Catholic Answers ↗).

Spurgeon’s original point was narrower. In his 1875 speech to the British and Foreign Bible Society, as transcribed on Wikiquote ↗, he argued for spreading and explaining the Bible rather than endlessly defending it: “The way to meet infidelity is to spread the Bible.”
context.pull: Open the door and let the lion out; he will take care of himself. — C. H. Spurgeon, 1875

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the quote under Augustine's Misattributed section, noting it is not found in his works and citing Spurgeon's 1875 Bible Society speech (5 May 1875, in Speeches at Home and Abroad, 1878) and the January 1888 sermon

Fauxtations (18 Oct 2015) searched CCEL and the Latin works (leo*/verita* in the same document 125 times, never close), found no Google Books reference before 2014, and first saw the quote on Facebook in 2013. It cites Spurgeon's 1875 speech and 1888 sermon but is not 100% certain they are the origin

Trent Horn, Catholic Answers, 8/3/2020: 'There is no way St. Augustine said this'. He found no book attributing it to Augustine before the twenty-first century, says Spurgeon's passage is strikingly similar but 'may not be the origin', and cites 1 Pet. 3:15

Spurgeon sermon No. 2004, 'The Lover of God's Law Filled with Peace', preached 22 January 1888 at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, Newington (Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit vol. 34), contains the caged-lion passage and 'lion-like majesty'
Fr. Brendan Lee, Jimboomba Times (25 June 2019), says Augustine never said this and calls the quote fake
